CausalChain: Hypoxia leads to HIF activation -> Upregulation of glycolytic enzymes (HK2, LDHA) elevates lactate production -> Excess lactate acidifies TME and signals via receptors (GPR81) -> Lactate drives macrophage polarization to M2 phenotype -> M2 macrophages secrete cytokines (e.g., IL-10, TGF-β) -> Cytokines stimulate upregulation of PHGDH and the serine synthesis pathway in tumor cells -> Enhanced serine metabolism boosts NADPH production -> Improved redox homeostasis promotes survival and drug resistance
Hypothesis: In hypoxic HCC, HIF-driven metabolic reprogramming results in elevated lactate production which, through lactate receptor engagement, polarizes TAMs toward an M2 phenotype. These M2 macrophages secrete specific cytokines that trigger a paracrine upregulation of the serine synthesis pathway (via PHGDH induction) in cancer cells, thereby enhancing NADPH production and supporting redox homeostasis. This metabolic adaptation is posited to underlie resistance to TKIs and ICIs. Given the complexity and interplay of these pathways, advanced tools such as single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial metabolomics, and CRISPR screens will be employed to delineate the mediators of this loop and to develop targeted interventions. Interruption of either lactate-induced macrophage signaling or the serine metabolism pathway is expected to disrupt this feedback mechanism and sensitizes HCC to therapy.
Abstract: We propose that in hypoxic hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), HIF-mediated upregulation of glycolytic enzymes (e.g., HK2, LDHA) leads to increased lactate production, which acidifies the tumor microenvironment and engages lactate receptors such as GPR81. This metabolic shift drives the polarization of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) toward an M2 phenotype. These M2 macrophages, characterized by a distinct secretory profile enriched in cytokines (for example, IL-10 and TGF-β), then facilitate a paracrine feedback loop that upregulates the serine synthesis pathway in adjacent tumor cells via enhanced PHGDH expression. The consequent elevation in serine metabolism boosts NADPH production essential for maintaining redox homeostasis, thereby conferring resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Utilizing modern technologies such as single-cell transcriptomics, spatial metabolomics, and CRISPR-based functional screening, this study aims to precisely identify the key mediators in this loop and validate therapeutic strategies targeting either lactate signaling or serine metabolic pathways to resensitize HCC cells to treatment.
Orignal_vs_New: The revised hypothesis maintains the original causal chain—starting from hypoxia-induced HIF activation and lactate production leading to M2 macrophage polarization, which in turn paracrinally upregulates the serine synthesis pathway to enhance NADPH-mediated redox balance and drug resistance. However, it clarifies the involvement of specific molecular players (e.g., HK2, LDHA, PHGDH, IL-10, and TGF-β) and explicitly integrates modern technological approaches (single-cell transcriptomics, spatial metabolomics, CRISPR screening) to validate and potentially target this feedback loop. These additions refine the mechanistic details and offer actionable experimental strategies, thereby enhancing the hypothesis’s scientific rigor and practical implementability.
